message: Can you read this ECG for me?
reply:
This is my read from the image only. I'm not a substitute for a clinician who knows the patient's history and symptoms.

## Interpretation

**Sinus rhythm at about 55–60 bpm (borderline sinus bradycardia), with left axis deviation consistent with left anterior fascicular block (LAFB), poor R-wave progression and nonspecific T-wave flattening.**

## Findings

| Feature | What I see |
|---|---|
| **Rate** | R-R interval is about 1.0–1.05 s (≈5 large boxes), so the rate is about **57–60 bpm** |
| **Rhythm** | Regular. Each QRS has an upright P wave before it in I and II, so it's **sinus** |
| **PR interval** | About 0.18–0.20 s. Normal to upper-normal, no clear AV block |
| **QRS duration** | Narrow, about 80–90 ms. No bundle branch block |
| **Axis** | **Left axis deviation, about −45°**: positive QRS in I, small rS in II, deep S in III and aVF, qR with a tall R in aVL |
| **Fascicular block** | qR in I/aVL plus rS in II/III/aVF plus left axis matches **LAFB** |
| **Voltage** | R in aVL is about 12 mm and R in I about 14 mm. aVL over 11 mm can be a voltage criterion for LVH, but LAFB inflates aVL, so this isn't reliable here |
| **R-wave progression** | rS in V1–V3, small RS in V4, transition around **V4–V5**. **Poor R-wave progression**, which is common with LAFB. It can also mean an old anterior MI or come from lead placement |
| **ST segments** | No clear ST elevation or depression |
| **T waves** | Upright in V2–V3. **Flat or low amplitude in I, aVL and V4–V6**, which is nonspecific |
| **QT** | About 0.38–0.40 s, so QTc is about 0.39–0.40 s. Normal |
| **Technical** | Lots of baseline noise in the limb leads (muscle tremor or artifact), which limits fine detail, especially of the P waves |

## Clinical notes
- Nothing here looks acute: no STEMI pattern and no high-grade block.
- LAFB on its own is usually benign, but it's often linked to hypertension, LVH or underlying coronary or conduction disease. An echo is reasonable if there's no prior workup.
- Comparing with a prior ECG would be the most useful next step, to tell whether the poor R-wave progression and T-wave changes are new.
- The bradycardia only matters if the patient has symptoms or is on rate-slowing drugs.

If you can share the clinical context (age, symptoms, why the ECG was done, any prior tracings), I can tighten up the interpretation.
